body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Wearable activity trackers with feedback after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Halvorsen-Mbeki T, Carrow-Adeyemi J, Lindqvist-Oduya P","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Joint Rehabilitation Research","doi":"10.5555/jjrr.2023.0217","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched five bibliographic databases from inception to March 2022 for randomised trials comparing activity tracker feedback with usual rehabilitation after primary total knee arthroplasty. Eleven trials with 1,146 participants met the criteria. Feedback increased daily step count at 12 weeks (mean difference 1,090 steps, 95 percent CI 540 to 1,640; eight trials) but did not clearly improve patient-reported function (standardised mean difference 0.12, 95 percent CI -0.05 to 0.29; nine trials). Heterogeneity was high for steps. Most trials were at some risk of bias from unblinded outcome assessment, and none reported results separately for patients over 75. Certainty was moderate for steps and low for function."},{"title":"Remote step-count feedback versus usual physiotherapy after knee replacement: a multicentre trial","authors":"Castell-Nwosu R, Brightman-Oyelaran K, Tanaka-Ferris D, Obi-Lundgren S","year":2021,"venue":"Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation","doi":"10.5555/cor.2021.0088","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Two hundred and twelve adults were randomly allocated after primary knee replacement to a wrist-worn tracker with weekly physiotherapist feedback on step targets or to usual physiotherapy. At 12 weeks the feedback group walked more (median 5,900 versus 4,700 steps per day), but the difference in patient-reported knee function was small and uncertain (2.1 points on a 48-point scale, 95 percent CI -0.8 to 5.0). Device wear on at least five days a week fell from 78 percent at week 6 to 61 percent at week 12. There were no differences in falls or readmissions. Physiotherapists spent a median of 4 minutes per patient per week on feedback."},{"title":"Who stops wearing it? Adherence to activity trackers among older adults after joint replacement","authors":"Ferreira-Doyle M, Asante-Kowalski B","year":2019,"venue":"Digital Health in Ageing","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 318 adults aged 65 and over who were given an activity tracker after hip or knee replacement and recorded whether data were synchronised each week for 12 weeks. Twenty-three percent never synchronised any data. Stopping within four weeks was more common in people aged over 80, people without a smartphone and people living alone. Patients who stopped reported difficulty charging the device, skin irritation and a sense that nobody looked at the data. The study could not tell whether stopping affected recovery, because function was not measured after discharge from the programme."},{"title":"Physiotherapist time spent reviewing remote activity data: a time-and-motion study in three orthopaedic services","authors":"Olumide-Sandberg E, Rourke-Achterberg N, Vasquez-Holm T","year":2022,"venue":"Physiotherapy Service Delivery","doi":"10.5555/psd.2022.0310","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Fourteen physiotherapists in three orthopaedic services recorded the time they spent on dashboards of patients' activity data after joint replacement over eight weeks. Reviewing the data and messaging patients took a median of 3.5 minutes per patient per week (interquartile range 2.0 to 6.0), with most time spent on patients whose step counts fell. Threshold alerts produced many prompts that led to no action, and two services switched them off. Physiotherapists valued the data for patients who lived far from the clinic but felt that reviews displaced face-to-face time when caseloads were high."},{"title":"Early walking volume and function six months after total knee replacement: a secondary analysis of exercise study data","authors":"Nakashima-Pryce A, Delacroix-Amadi O","year":2016,"venue":"Knee Outcomes Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using step counts recorded in the sixth week after surgery by 406 participants of an exercise study, we examined whether walking volume predicted patient-reported function at six months. Each additional 1,000 steps per day was associated with a 1.4-point better function score, but the association fell to 0.5 points (95 percent CI -0.2 to 1.2) after adjustment for pre-operative function and pain. Walking volume may mark recovery rather than cause it, so raising step counts alone may not improve function. Participants were younger and fitter than typical surgical patients."},{"title":"Rapid reviews for hospital technology decisions: agreement with full systematic reviews on the direction of effect","authors":"Whitcombe-Eze L, Sorensen-Baptiste H, Quayle-Moreno R","year":2020,"venue":"Evidence Synthesis Methods Notes","doi":"10.5555/esmn.2020.0045","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 30 rapid reviews produced for hospital technology decisions with full systematic reviews on the same questions. Conclusions agreed on the direction of effect in 27 of 30 pairs. Rapid reviews more often missed non-English and grey literature and less often reported a risk of bias assessment. Disagreements arose where the evidence base was small or changing quickly. We recommend that rapid reviews state every shortcut taken, date their searches and say which conclusions would change if a missed study pointed the other way."},{"title":"Being watched or being supported? Patients' experience of app-based activity feedback in knee rehabilitation","authors":"Mbatha-Rowntree C, Ekstrom-Idowu F","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Joint Rehabilitation Research","doi":"10.5555/jjrr.2024.0102","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 22 patients who had used an activity tracker with physiotherapist feedback for 12 weeks after knee replacement. Most valued seeing their progress and said that messages from a named physiotherapist kept them walking. Several felt judged by daily step targets on days when pain or swelling limited walking, and some stopped wearing the device after a week of low counts. Patients in areas with poor mobile coverage described missed synchronisation and repeated reminders. Participants asked for targets that could be adjusted and for someone to explain what the data were used for."}]}
